extracted.intended_audience: litigators and judges in patent venue/transfer disputes (district & appellate counsel)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and criteria for seeking mandamus relief to review a district court's decision denying transfer under 28 U.S.C. § 1404(a), including how appellate review applies regional circuit law and how district courts should weigh traditional transfer factors in patent cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mandamus elements (Cheney)
rubrics_metrics.description: To obtain a writ of mandamus, a petitioner must show that: (1) it has a clear and indisputable right to relief; (2) it does not have any other adequate method of obtaining relief; and (3) the 'writ is appropriate under the circumstances.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mandamus is 'reserved for extraordinary situations.' (Gulfstream Aerospace). The petition must meet all three Cheney factors; mere disagreement with the district court is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard for mandamus review of §1404(a) transfers (regional circuit law)
rubrics_metrics.description: When evaluating transfer decisions under 28 U.S.C. § 1404(a), appellate courts generally apply the law of the regional circuit in which the district court sits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under Fifth Circuit law (applicable here), mandamus may be granted only for 'a clear abuse of discretion such that refusing transfer produced a patently erroneous result.' (In re TS Tech USA Corp.). Thus appellate relief is available only in extraordinary, fact-specific circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good-cause requirement under Fifth Circuit
rubrics_metrics.description: The movant must demonstrate 'good cause' for transfer under the governing Fifth Circuit standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A district court may deny transfer where it finds relevant contacts (e.g., significant operations, witnesses, or proof) in the transferor forum; the movant must provide sufficiently compelling reasons to show the transferee forum is clearly more convenient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Willing witness factor (convenience of witnesses)
rubrics_metrics.description: The willing witness factor examines where witnesses with relevant and material information are located and whether they are willing to testify.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A court should consider which employees or third parties possess relevant, material information (including hardware, server-side, or software aspects where relevant). The district court here found five Apple employees in Austin knowledgeable about accused products and weighed that against transfer. A party asserting those witnesses are irrelevant must show why (e.g., by tying the asserted claim scope to only software features).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope-of-claims relevance inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: The court should assess the scope of the asserted claims and the information in possession of identified employees to determine whether hardware or server-side functionality is relevant to infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if a party argues the case is limited to software, the district court may find hardware or server-side functionality potentially relevant after examining claim scope and employee knowledge. Appellate review is deferential on these fact-intensive determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compulsory process factor
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether the transferee forum's compulsory process will be more effective in securing unwilling witnesses or evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The district court here found the compulsory process factor slightly weighed against transfer. Movants should identify specific witnesses who are unwilling to testify absent compulsory process and explain where compulsory process would be beneficial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification of specific third-party/unwilling witnesses
rubrics_metrics.description: A movant should identify any specific third-party individuals in the transferee forum who are unwilling to testify (or otherwise unavailable) to support a transfer request.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court criticized Apple's failure to identify any specific third-party individuals in Northern California who were unwilling to testify; absent such specifics, courts are unlikely to credit speculative assertions of inconvenience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources of proof location
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider where documentary and physical sources of proof were created and are maintained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The district court found sources of proof were created and maintained in both forums; when sources are split between forums, that factor may be neutral. Movants should provide evidence tying documents and data to a particular forum to gain weight on this factor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Location of relevant operations / product development
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess where the accused products were manufactured, developed, or where relevant company operations are located.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Here the district court found Apple had significant relevant operations in Austin, where some accused products were manufactured and developed, which weighed against transfer. Movants should identify specific operations and tie them to alleged infringement activities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost-to-attend-trial and convenience for key parties/witnesses
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate relative travel costs and convenience for key witnesses, parties, and the inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court noted the cost of attending trial in Austin would be less for the inventor residing in New York. Consider travel burden for material witnesses and parties when arguing convenience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of unnamed team members / vague witnesses
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts may refuse to credit unnamed or vaguely-described team members absent information about what relevant and material information they possess.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apple identified additional unnamed Northern California team members but provided little information about what relevant information they would provide; the district court reasonably declined to credit them. Movants should provide particularized info about unnamed persons if relying on them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance-of-factors / overall convenience calculus
rubrics_metrics.description: The district court must weigh all traditional transfer factors together and conclude whether the transferee forum is 'clearly more convenient.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many factors may be neutral; on balance the movant must demonstrate the transferee forum is clearly more convenient. Absent a compelling imbalance, courts deny transfer. Appellate mandamus relief requires that the district court's balancing be a clear abuse producing a patently erroneous result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deference to district-court fact-intensive determinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Appellate review of transfer denials is highly deferential because determinations are fact-intensive and entrusted principally to the district court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citations: In re Vistaprint Ltd. Appellate courts will not overturn fact-bound assessments unless they constitute clear error or produce a patently erroneous result under the regional-circuit mandamus standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mootness of stay request after written decision
rubrics_metrics.description: If the district court issues a written transfer decision, a petition requesting a stay pending that written decision may become moot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Here, because the district court issued its written decision denying transfer, Apple's request for a stay pending issuance of that decision was moot.
